The Free Soil Party. It was a short-lived antislavery political movement of the 1848 to 1854 era, formed by Northern Democrats opposed to slavery expansion into western territories. Running on the slogan "Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor," it would later merge into the nascent Republican Party, making it a crucial bridge between the Whigs and the GOP.

The party emerged from a coalition of Barnburner Democrats—radical New York Democrats opposed to slavery—and some antislavery Whigs and Liberty Party members. Rather than demanding slavery's abolition in existing states, the Free Soilers opposed slavery's expansion into new territories. They framed this as a matter of free labor competition and worker rights rather than moral abolition.

Former President Martin Van Buren became the party's 1848 presidential candidate. His candidacy split the Democratic vote, contributing to Whig Zachary Taylor's election. Van Buren won nearly 10 percent of the popular vote, establishing the party as a significant force. The Free Soil platform held that new Western lands should be reserved for free Northern settlers and laborers, not slaveholders and enslaved workers.

After the 1848 election, Free Soilers elected several representatives and maintained a presence in Congress. John C. Fremont, a Free Soil notable, would become the Republican Party's first presidential nominee in 1856. The party dissolved by the mid-1850s as most members joined the new Republican Party, which absorbed the Free Soil program of opposing slavery's territorial expansion. In this way, the Free Soil movement became one of the most influential third parties in American history, fundamentally shaping the major-party realignment that preceded the Civil War.
